subject: grid argument in the akde function

messages.author: 6f84786b4d90ec96
messages.subject: grid argument in the akde function
parts:
Perhaps I misunderstand the grid argument in the akde function but I thought that if grid was equal to a consistent extent for all akde's then all akde's would be placed on a common grid.

# CTMM version 0.5.11  

In my case, I am using an extent named ee1.

> ee1
             x         y
min -142294.49 -26822.12
max   58180.37 103601.34

I then run all akde's with grid=ee1.

> akde1=akde(data[1],fitModels[1],grid=ee1)
> akde2=akde(data[2],fitModels[2],grid=ee1)

But when I run the overlap function it returns an error that "inconsistent grid resolutions" or "non-conformable arrays" depending upon which version of ctmm I am using

> overlap(c(akde1,akde2),level=0.95)
Error in grid.intersection(UD) : Inconsistent grid resolutions.

Sure enough the grid extents are not the same?

> ee1
             x         y
min -142294.49 -26822.12
max   58180.37 103601.34

> extent(akde1)
            x         y
min -18102.06  3153.251
max -11164.60 12370.169

> extent(akde2)
             x         y
min -21819.422 -15817.64
max   8333.301  14886.21 

Any idea what I am doing wrong?  Is there a different way in which the grid argument should be defined?

I have over 150 akde's to produce and have ran them using a foreach command to fully utilize my computers resources and make processing time greatly reduced.  I understand that if I run:

> akde1=akde(data[1:2],fitModels[1:2])

that these two akde's will be placed on the same grid.

Any help is much appreciated.

Best,

Matt Butler

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: grid argument in the akde function
parts:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

Hi Kristin,

The easiest way to calculate your UDs in the same grid is to calculate them in one call like akde(TELEMETRY_LIST,FIT_LIST). This will work fine as long as the home ranges aren't radically different sizes.

Best,
Chris

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

Chris

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Chris

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

Follow up to my overlapping home ranges question! 

I found that many of my cats constrict or expand their home range seasonally, but don't actually shift very far. So a low overlap percentage doesn't necessarily tell me that they moved to a new area, just that their two home ranges overlap minimally. Attached plot show 4 years of winter - to - summer overlap comparisons for the same cat. Only in 2023 does it look like she actually shifted her range. My next thought was that I should look at mean centroid shifts between home ranges as part of the decision process to classify if a cat shifted vs expanded/constricted (if their overlap is small). 

I used ctmm::distance on the FITS objects for each site (as we talked about above), like this:
books_distances <- ctmm::distance(FITS.books, method="Euclidean",  sqrt=TRUE) 

However, all the values are absolutely massive. I tested both  sqrt=TRUE and  sqrt=FALSE, which gave me the same values. After cleaning up the resulting matrices so I only had pairwise comparisons between the same individuals's various seasons, I divided the values by 1e+6 (assuming it was in sq m) to get sq km.

However, the distance given for that same pairwise comparison is 2.219973e+10, which (if is supposed to be meters), would be 22,199.73 sq km. That is clearly not correct. 

I think this means I did something wrong in fitting the distance() function, so I was hoping you could see a glaring issue that I missed :D 
Thanks for all your help!!

Kristin

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris

On Sat, Oct 17, 2020 at 11:11 AM Christen Fleming <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Matt,

The grid argument can take a lot of different options, but with just an extent it isn't going to be fully specified, because the resolutions can still differ. I checked my code and, not being fully specified, the extents weren't being set exactly, so I fixed that on GitHub, but it's probably not what you wanted. You probably wanted to do something more like grid=list(extent=ee1,dr=500), for instance, if you wanted 500 meter resolution. The newer code on GitHub is also more memory efficient in that you can do something like grid=list(dr=500,align.to.origin=TRUE), to calculate overlaps with smaller grids with cells that line up but the grids don't have to be all encompassing any longer.

The extent() function on UD objects has confidence and coverage level arguments, because it's designed more for lining up plots, so those aren't going to necessarily going to return the same values. What you would want to check is the range of UD$r$x and UD$r$y, which are the grid coordinates, but with the newer code on GitHub only the resolution and offset needs to be the same.

Best,
Chris
